title: Fix WatchGlobalProcessInfo infinite retry on service incarnation mismatch
body:
Fix WatchGlobalProcessInfo infinite retry on service incarnation mismatch

When the coordination service restarts, surviving tasks hold a stale
service incarnation ID. Their WatchTasksAsync RPCs fail with
"wrong service incarnation", and the WatchGlobalProcessInfo loop
retries indefinitely because it never checks the agent error state.

Check agent.IsError() after a failed WatchTasksAsync. If the agent
has entered an unrecoverable ERROR state (set by the WatchTasksAsync
callback on incarnation mismatch), return the error instead of
retrying. Transient errors that do not trigger SetError continue
to be retried.

title: Avoid grabbing the `TileAssignment` mutex in the common case.
body:
Avoid grabbing the `TileAssignment` mutex in the common case.

Before this change, many trivial accessor fuctions in `TileAssignment`
would acquire the mutex protecting the materialized array. This is
especially unfortunate for accessors like `num_dimensions()`, which can
be called in loops and which should always be able to obtain the value
cheaply (without acquiring any locks) from either `iota_` or the
materialized array.

This change makes `array_` an atomic pointer to enable it to be accessed
without locking. Accessors that can use either `iota_` or `array_` are
changed to try `iota_` by default unless obtaining the value from
`array_` is cheaper. After this change, the mutex is only acquired when
we materialize the array or access `shared_array_`.

title: Add Variable slice assignment feature
body:
## Description

This PR implements Python syntactic sugar for `tf.Variable` slice assignments, allowing users to seamlessly assign values to variable slices using `__setitem__`.

Previously, attempting `A[:2, :2] = ...` on a variable would result in `TypeError: 'ResourceVariable' object does not support item assignment`. Users had to manually use `A[:2, :2].assign(...)`. This PR bridges the gap in user experience, providing parity with PyTorch mutable tensors (as requested in Issue #33131).

## Changes made
- Added `_setitem_helper_var(var, slice_spec, value)` in `tensorflow/python/ops/tensor_getitem_override.py`. This function intercepts the `__setitem__` call and routes it directly to the `.assign()` method of the underlying `_SliceHelperVar` object.
- Registered `__setitem__` inside `Variable._OverloadAllOperators` (`tensorflow/python/ops/variables.py`) to map to the new helper function.
- Added a new unit test `testSliceAssignment` to `VariablesTestCase` (`tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/variables/variables_test.py`) to ensure flawless execution in both eager and graph modes.

## Example Usage
```python
import tensorflow as tf

A = tf.Variable([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]], dtype=tf.float32)

# New Syntactic Sugar!
A[:2, :2] = 22. * tf.ones((2, 2))

print(A.numpy())
# [[22. 22.  3.]
#  [22. 22.  6.]
#  [ 7.  8.  9.]]

title: Fix host memory leak in tf.data.Dataset.from_generator during eager execution
body:
## Bug fix: host RAM leak in `tf.data.Dataset.from_generator` (#123269)

**Reproduction:** Running `from_generator` in a loop leaks ~128 MB of host RSS over 500 iterations even after `del dataset` and `gc.collect()`. GPU VRAM is unaffected.

## Root cause

Every call to `from_generator` traces three closures via `StructuredFunctionWrapper` (`init_func`, `next_func`, `finalize_func`). During tracing those closures call `numpy_function` / `eager_py_func`, which routes through `_internal_py_func` in `script_ops.py`. There, a **strong reference** to each closure is stored:

```python
# script_ops.py – the leak
graph = ops.get_default_graph()
while True:          # walk up to outermost non-FuncGraph
    ...
graph._py_funcs_used_in_graph.append(func)   # ← accumulates forever
```

In eager mode the outermost non-FuncGraph is the **process-lifetime singleton** returned by `ops.get_default_graph()`. It is never destroyed, so `_py_funcs_used_in_graph` grows indefinitely. After 500 iterations, ~1 500 closures accumulate there (each capturing a `generator_state` object), accounting for the ~128 MB RSS growth.

## Fix

When `_internal_py_func` is called while already executing inside a `FuncGraph` (as happens during `StructuredFunctionWrapper` tracing), skip the walk-to-outermost-graph and keep the strong reference on the **FuncGraph itself**:

```python
if not isinstance(graph, func_graph.FuncGraph):
    while True:   # only walk up when NOT already in a FuncGraph
        ...
graph._py_funcs_used_in_graph.append(func)
```

The `FuncGraph`'s lifetime is tied to its `ConcreteFunction` → `StructuredFunctionWrapper` → `Dataset`. When `del dataset` runs and GC collects the chain, the `FuncGraph` is dismantled, `_py_funcs_used_in_graph` on it is released, and all three closures (and their `generator_state` captures) are freed.

In graph mode and in eager mode outside any `FuncGraph` the original behaviour is preserved unchanged.

Fixes #123269

title: Fix tf.raw_ops.RFFT crashing on fft_length=[0] instead of raising InvalidArgumentError
body:
## Bug fix: `tf.raw_ops.RFFT` with `fft_length=[0]` crashes the process

Fixes #123399

**Reproduction:**
```python
x = tf.fill([3, 3, 31], tf.constant(-1.0, dtype=tf.float32))
y = tf.raw_ops.RFFT(input=x, fft_length=tf.constant([0], dtype=tf.int32))
tf.shape(y).numpy()
# Aborted (core dumped) — DUCC FFT assertion: "axis length mismatch"
```

## Root cause

The input validation in `fft_ops.cc` checked `fft_length[i] >= 0`, allowing `fft_length=0` to pass through. With an FFT size of 0, the output shape is set to `[3, 3, 0]` and the call is forwarded to the DUCC FFT library, which fatally aborts with a C-level assertion instead of raising a recoverable Python exception.

## Fix

Change the guard in `fft_ops.cc` from `>= 0` to `> 0` and update the error message accordingly:

```cpp
// Before
OP_REQUIRES(ctx, fft_length_as_vec(i) >= 0,
            errors::InvalidArgument("fft_length[", i, "] must >= 0 ..."));

// After
OP_REQUIRES(ctx, fft_length_as_vec(i) > 0,
            errors::InvalidArgument("fft_length[", i, "] must be > 0 ..."));
```

After the fix, calling with `fft_length=[0]` raises a clean `InvalidArgumentError` before reaching the FFT kernel.

## Test

Added `test_zero_fft_length_raises` to `fft_ops_test.py` targeting `gen_spectral_ops.r_f_f_t` directly (the high-level `tf.signal.rfft` wrapper applies its own constraints and does not exercise this validation path).

title: [PJRT] Add support for UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer and CommonPjRtClient::MakeUndonatable.
body:
[PJRT] Add support for UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer and CommonPjRtClient::MakeUndonatable.

Provide a factory `MakeUndonatable` for turning an existing buffer into an `UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer`, it consumes the input buffer and returns an equivalent hold-free buffer aliasing the same device memory. It uses CommonPjRtClient's friend access on CommonPjRtBuffer to donate the tracked buffer, snapshotting the underlying raw buffer along with its definition events to construct UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer.

Static factory `UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer::Create` is provided as a helper on the buffer class that delegates to `CommonPjRtClient::MakeUndonatable`. Unit tests in `undonatable_common_pjrt_buffer_test.cc` have been updated to use the factory and include null-check verification.

title: PR #45263: Allow dynamic-update-slice into an unbounded-dynamic operand dimension
body:
PR #45263: Allow dynamic-update-slice into an unbounded-dynamic operand dimension

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45263

### Problem
`InferDynamicUpdateSliceShape` rejects a valid `dynamic-update-slice` into an **unbounded-dynamic** operand dimension.

### Root cause
```cpp
const int64_t input_dim_size = operand_shape.dimensions(dim);
...
if (update_dim_size > input_dim_size) {   // input_dim_size == kUnboundedSize (INT64_MIN) for an unbounded dim
  return InvalidArgument("Update dim size %d greater than dynamic slice dimension: %d.", ...);
}
```
For an unbounded-dynamic operand dimension, `operand_shape.dimensions(dim)` is `kUnboundedSize` (`INT64_MIN`). Any concrete static update size (e.g. `5`) then satisfies `5 > INT64_MIN` and the op is rejected with a nonsensical bound (`-9223372036854775808`). The sibling `InferDynamicSliceShape` guards the identical comparison with `!IsUnboundedDynamicSize(input_dim_size)`, and this function already handles unbounded *update* sizes just above — so unbounded operands are in scope, but the operand side is unguarded.

### Fix
Guard with `!IsUnboundedDynamicSize(input_dim_size)`, matching `InferDynamicSliceShape`.

### Verification
Static reasoning: e.g. `operand = f32[?, 10]`, `update = f32[3, 5]` is rejected today (`3 > INT64_MIN`) and accepted with the fix; operand-static-with-too-large-update still errors; both-unbounded and operand-static-with-unbounded-update are unchanged. (No local Bazel build set up — happy to add a shape-inference test.)

Copybara import of the project:

--
1b4c86365393d200d45a372af006ea0a64b94a74 by Eylon Krause <eylon1909@gmail.com>:

Allow dynamic-update-slice into an unbounded-dynamic operand dimension

InferDynamicUpdateSliceShape rejected a static update dimension larger than
the operand dimension, but for an unbounded-dynamic operand dimension
operand_shape.dimensions(dim) is kUnboundedSize (INT64_MIN), so any concrete
update size trivially exceeds it and a valid op is rejected with a
nonsensical bound. Guard the comparison with
!IsUnboundedDynamicSize(input_dim_size), matching the sibling
InferDynamicSliceShape.


Merging this change closes #45263

title: SIGFPE in SequenceExample parsing with FixedLenSequenceFeature shape=[0]
body:
### Issue type

Bug

### Have you reproduced the bug with TensorFlow Nightly?

Yes

### Source

source

### TensorFlow version

tf.version.VERSION: 2.21.0-dev0+selfbuilt

### Custom code

Yes

### OS platform and distribution

Linux Ubuntu 22.04

### Mobile device

_No response_

### Python version

Python 3.10.12

### Bazel version

bazel-9.1.0

### GCC/compiler version

gcc (Ubuntu 11.4.0-1ubuntu1~22.04.2) 11.4.0

### CUDA/cuDNN version

_No response_

### GPU model and memory

_No response_

### Current behavior?

Calling TensorFlow SequenceExample parsing APIs with a FixedLenSequenceFeature whose shape contains a zero dimension can trigger a SIGFPE in TensorFlow's native fast parsing path.

I observed the same underlying crash through three public TensorFlow APIs:

tf.io.FixedLenSequenceFeature
tf.io.parse_sequence_example
tf.io.parse_single_sequence_example

These appear to be different entry points into the same root cause. In all cases, the crash points to TensorFlow's native ParseSequenceDenseFeatures implementation:

example_proto_fast_parsing.cc
tensorflow::example::(anonymous namespace)::ParseSequenceDenseFeatures(...)

The minimal reproducer below uses tf.io.parse_single_sequence_example with an empty SequenceExample and a single sequence feature spec:

sequence_features = {
    "k": tf.io.FixedLenSequenceFeature(
        shape=[0],
        dtype=tf.float32,
        allow_missing=True,
    )
}

In my ASan-enabled TensorFlow build, this does not fail with a clean, catchable TensorFlow exception. Instead, the process aborts with an AddressSanitizer FPE report in ParseSequenceDenseFeatures.

This can cause a denial-of-service condition when SequenceExample feature specifications are derived from malformed or untrusted input. A zero dimension in FixedLenSequenceFeature.shape should be rejected deterministically before entering the native fast parser, preferably with a recoverable Python exception such as InvalidArgumentError.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import tensorflow as tf

serialized = tf.train.SequenceExample().SerializeToString()

sequence_features = {
    "k": tf.io.FixedLenSequenceFeature(
        shape=[0],
        dtype=tf.float32,
        allow_missing=True,
    )
}

tf.io.parse_single_sequence_example(
    serialized=serialized,
    sequence_features=sequence_features,
)
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
AddressSanitizer:DEADLYSIGNAL

title: PR #45816: [XLA:GPU] Don't let rank-0 dimension-size scalars inherit op sharding
body:
PR #45816: [XLA:GPU] Don't let rank-0 dimension-size scalars inherit op sharding

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45816

📝 Summary of Changes
Stop rank-0 dimension-size scalars from inheriting the enclosing op's sharding.

🎯 Justification
Shardy-partitioned MoE models (MaxText Mixtral, DeepSeek2, GPT-OSS) fail to compile. Their bf16 top-k routing lowers into an op that, under a tiled sharding, passes a multi-dimensional sharding onto a scalar, which is invalid and aborts compilation. This has been latent and only surfaced after this #44538

🚀 Kind of Contribution
🐛 Bug Fix

🧪 Unit Tests:
New case in `mhlo_to_hlo/tests/sharding.mlir`
Copybara import of the project:

--
e12c6475bdd83bfa3871338257b0308f925065a4 by Aleksei Nurmukhametov <anurmukh@amd.com>:

[XLA:GPU] Don't let rank-0 dimension-size scalars inherit op sharding

RemoveDynamicDimension/GetDimensionSize create a rank-0 constant to hold the
static size. The mhlo->hlo op writer applies each op's mhlo.sharding to
everything created while lowering that op, so under a rank>0 tiled sharding
the scalar picks it up and HloSharding::Validate fails. Clear the
sharding around the constant as other builder helpers do.


Merging this change closes #45816

title: Fix heap out-of-bounds write in CTCLoss when U=1.
body:
Fix heap out-of-bounds write in CTCLoss when U=1.

The `CTCLossCalculator` initialization logic assumed `U >= 2`, leading to invalid memory access in `CalculateForwardVariables` and `CalculateBackwardVariables` when the target sequence collapses to an empty sequence (`U=1`).

- In `CalculateForwardVariables`, unconditional access to `log_alpha->coeffRef(1, 0)` is now guarded with `if (U > 1)`.
- In `CalculateBackwardVariables`, the lower bound of the initialization loop is now clamped using `std::max(0, U - 2)` to prevent negative index access.

title: Fix heap out-of-bounds write in CTC loss with empty target sequence
body:
### Summary

Fixes #123396 — a heap out-of-bounds write in the native CTC loss CPU
implementation that AddressSanitizer reports as a `bad-free` when calling
`tf.raw_ops.CTCLoss` with a minimal single-class configuration.

### Root cause

`CTCLossOp` hardcodes the blank label as `num_classes - 1`. With
`inputs` shape `[1, 1, 1]`, `num_classes == 1`, so the blank index is `0`.
A label value of `0` therefore equals the blank and is treated as a
"null/finished" label in `PopulateLPrimes`, collapsing the target to an
empty sequence. `GetLPrimeIndices` then produces `l_prime = [blank]`, so
`U = l_prime.size() == 1`.

Two initialization sites in `ctc_loss_calculator.h` assume `U >= 2` and
write outside the `U x T` (here `1 x 1`) alpha/beta matrices:

- `CalculateForwardVariables` unconditionally wrote `log_alpha->coeffRef(1, 0)`
  (row 1 of a 1-row matrix). The surrounding code already anticipated
  `U == 1` via the `l_prime.size() > 1 ? l_prime[1] : blank_index_` ternary,
  but the write itself was not guarded.
- `CalculateBackwardVariables` looped `for (int u = U - 2; u < U; ++u)`,
  starting at `u == -1` and writing `log_beta->coeffRef(-1, T - 1)`.

Both are heap out-of-bounds writes that corrupt the Eigen matrix
allocation metadata, later surfacing as the ASan `bad-free`.

### Fix

Complete the already-intended `U == 1` handling:

- Guard the second-row `log_alpha` initialization behind `if (U > 1)`.
- Clamp the `log_beta` initialization lower bound with `std::max(0, U - 2)`.

The degenerate empty-target case now computes a finite loss
(`-log P(all blanks)`) and gradient instead of corrupting the heap. The
`U > 1` path is unchanged.

### Test

Adds `testSingleClassBlankOnlyLabel` to `ctc_loss_op_test.py`, which
reproduces the exact minimal input from the issue and asserts a finite
loss and gradient of the expected shapes. Runs in both graph and eager
modes. Without the fix this test crashes the process under ASan; with it,
it passes.

### Notes

- No API or behavioral change for valid CTC inputs; only the previously
  crashing degenerate case is affected.
- CLA: signed.

title: reject empty row_splits when decoding RaggedTensorVariant

labels.name: comp:core
labels.description: issues related to core part of tensorflow

body: RaggedComponentsFromVariant checks a decoded component's row_splits dtype and rank but never that the tensor is non-empty, so a variant carrying a row_splits of shape [0] gets through. NestedStackRaggedTensors then sizes the stacked splits tensor with `splits(i).NumElements() - 1` per component, which contributes -1 for that component while the write loop below it contributes no writes, so the allocation ends up one element short per empty component and the loop writes past the end with attacker-controlled values; two or more make split_size negative and TensorShape CHECK-fails. RaggedTensorVerifySplits in ragged_utils.h already rejects empty splits and RaggedTensorToVariant runs it on the encode side, so this only rejects inputs the encoder could never have produced.

title: PR #45821: [HLO] Validate the dimensions attribute in the HLO parser to avoid crashes
body:
PR #45821: [HLO] Validate the dimensions attribute in the HLO parser to avoid crashes

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45821

### Problem
Several opcode handlers extract or use a value from the `dimensions={...}` attribute without validating it, so malformed-but-lexable HLO text crashes the parser (a `std::out_of_range` throw, an out-of-bounds read, or a `CHECK`-fail) instead of returning an error `Status`.

**Empty `dimensions={}`** — `all-gather`, `all-gather-start`, `reduce-scatter`, and `get-dimension-size` / `set-dimension-size` extract `dimensions->at(0)`, but the parser only checks that the required attribute is *present*, not non-empty. An empty list therefore throws `std::out_of_range`:
```
all-gather(input), replica_groups={}, dimensions={}
reduce-scatter(input), replica_groups={}, to_apply=add, dimensions={}
get-dimension-size(p), dimensions={}
```

**Out-of-range dimension value** — `scan` checks `dimensions->size() == 1` but then uses the value as `operands[0]->shape().dimensions(scan_dim)` with no range check, so an out-of-range value reads out of bounds (and the downstream `ShapeUtil::InsertDimensionAtIndex` `CHECK`-fails):
```
scan(input, init), dimensions={-1}, num_carries=0, to_apply=add
```

### Fix
- Require `dimensions->size() == 1` in the all-gather / reduce-scatter / get-dimension-size / set-dimension-size handlers before extracting `dimensions->at(0)`, matching the checks the sibling `kSort` and `kAllToAll` handlers already have. (`all-reduce`/`all-reduce-start` share the reduce-scatter parse block and don't take a `dimensions` attribute, so the new check is guarded by `opcode == kReduceScatter`.)
- Range-check `scan`'s dimension against the operand rank and return a parse error if it is out of range.

### Tests
Four `HloParserTest` cases assert that `all-gather`, `reduce-scatter`, and `get-dimension-size` with `dimensions={}`, and `scan` with an out-of-range dimension, now return an error instead of crashing.

---
Disclosure: this contribution was authored with an AI coding assistant (Claude) and reviewed before submission.

If your company or organization uses Python and would benefit from HTTP/2 support in Requests, pip, cloud SDKs, and thousands of other projects please consider contributing financially to ensure HTTP/2 support is developed sustainably and maintained for the long-haul.

Thank you for your support.

Security

Addressed high-severity security issues. Impact was limited to specific use cases detailed in the accompanying advisories; overall user exposure was estimated to be marginal.

  • Decompression-bomb safeguards of the streaming API were bypassed:

    1. When HTTPResponse.drain_conn() was called after the response had been read and decompressed partially. (Reported by @​Cycloctane)
    2. During the second HTTPResponse.read(amt=N) or HTTPResponse.stream(amt=N) call when the response was decompressed using the official Brotli library. (Reported by @​kimkou2024)

    See GHSA-mf9v-mfxr-j63j for details.

  • HTTP pools created using ProxyManager.connection_from_url did not strip sensitive headers specified in Retry.remove_headers_on_redirect when redirecting to a different host. (GHSA-qccp-gfcp-xxvc reported by @​christos-spearbit)

Deprecations and Removals

  • Used FutureWarning instead of DeprecationWarning for better visibility of existing deprecation notices. Rescheduled the removal of deprecated features to version 3.0. (urllib3/urllib3#3763)
  • Removed support for end-of-life Python 3.9. (urllib3/urllib3#3720)
  • Removed support for end-of-life PyPy3.10. (urllib3/urllib3#4979)
  • Bumped the minimum supported pyOpenSSL version to 19.0.0. (urllib3/urllib3#3777)

Bugfixes

  • Fixed a bug where HTTPResponse.read(amt=None) was ignoring decompressed data buffered from previous partial reads. (urllib3/urllib3#3636)
  • Fixed a bug where HTTPResponse.read() could cache only part of the response after a partial read when cache_content=True. (urllib3/urllib3#4967)
  • Fixed HTTPResponse.stream() and HTTPResponse.read_chunked() to handle amt=0. (urllib3/urllib3#3793)
  • Updated _TYPE_BODY type alias to include missing Iterable[str], matching the documented and runtime behavior of chunked request bodies. (urllib3/urllib3#3798)
  • Fixed LocationParseError when paths resembling schemeless URIs were passed to HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen(). (urllib3/urllib3#3352)
  • Fixed BaseHTTPResponse.readinto() type annotation to accept memoryview in addition to bytearray, matching the io.RawIOBase.readinto contract and enabling use with io.BufferedReader without type errors. (urllib3/urllib3#3764)

title: [IFRT] Copy serialized Cord to std::string during deserialization to avoid ASan buffer overflow
body:
[IFRT] Copy serialized Cord to std::string during deserialization to avoid ASan buffer overflow

MLIR Lexer (used by the text/assembly parser) assumes the input buffer is null-terminated. When parsing text-based StableHLO or IFRT IR during deserialization, `deserializePortableArtifact` and `ParseMlirModuleString` receive a non-null-terminated `absl::string_view` from `absl::Cord::Flatten()`. If an identifier ends exactly at the buffer boundary, the lexer reads past the end of the buffer, causing an ASan `stack-buffer-overflow`.

To fix this safely across remaining callsites, we copy the serialized data to a `std::string` to guarantee null-termination before passing it to MLIR parsing or string parsing utilities.

### Current behavior?

Calling tf.raw_ops.RFFT with fft_length=[0] can crash the TensorFlow process instead of raising a clean Python-level TensorFlow exception.

The reproducer below uses only a small dense input tensor and a one-element FFT length tensor:

input dtype:  tf.float32
fft_length:   [0]

In my latest TensorFlow build, this input does not fail with a recoverable InvalidArgumentError. Instead, the process terminates with a fatal signal.

This is similar in spirit to previous TensorFlow signal-op input validation issues, but this reproducer uses the 1D raw op tf.raw_ops.RFFT directly. A zero FFT length should be rejected deterministically before entering the FFT kernel.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import tensorflow as tf

x = tf.fill([3, 3, 31], tf.constant(-1.0, dtype=tf.float32))
fft_length = tf.constant([0], dtype=tf.int32)

y = tf.raw_ops.RFFT(
    input=x,
    fft_length=fft_length,
)

tf.shape(y).numpy()
```

### GPU model and memory

_No response_

### Current behavior?

Calling tf.raw_ops.CropAndResizeGradImage with a rank-1 empty boxes tensor can crash the TensorFlow process instead of raising a clean, catchable TensorFlow exception.

The reproducer below uses only very small tensors:

grads shape:      [0, 1, 1, 1]
boxes shape:      [0]
box_ind shape:    [0]
image_size:       [2, 7, 7, 1]
T:                tf.float32
method:           "bilinear"

Here, boxes is an empty rank-1 tensor:

boxes = tf.constant([], dtype=tf.float32)

For CropAndResizeGradImage, boxes is expected to represent crop boxes, so an empty valid boxes tensor would normally have shape [0, 4]. A rank-1 empty tensor with shape [0] is malformed and should be rejected deterministically.

In my latest TensorFlow build, this input does not fail with a recoverable Python-level exception such as InvalidArgumentError. Instead, the process terminates with a fatal signal.

This can cause a denial-of-service condition when CropAndResizeGradImage receives malformed crop metadata derived from untrusted input. Invalid boxes shapes should be rejected before entering the native image-gradient kernel path.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import tensorflow as tf

grads = tf.zeros([0, 1, 1, 1], dtype=tf.float32)
boxes = tf.constant([], dtype=tf.float32)
box_ind = tf.constant([], dtype=tf.int32)
image_size = tf.constant([2, 7, 7, 1], dtype=tf.int32)

y = tf.raw_ops.CropAndResizeGradImage(
    grads=grads,
    boxes=boxes,
    box_ind=box_ind,
    image_size=image_size,
    T=tf.float32,
    method="bilinear",
)

tf.reduce_sum(y).numpy()

gcc (Ubuntu 11.4.0-1ubuntu1~22.04.2) 11.4.0

### CUDA/cuDNN version

_No response_

### GPU model and memory

_No response_

### Current behavior?

Calling tf.raw_ops.CTCLoss with a minimal valid-looking CTC configuration can trigger an ASan-detected bad-free in the native CTC loss implementation.

The reproducer below uses only a very small input tensor and one label entry:

inputs = [[[-1.0]]]
labels_indices = [[0, 0]]
labels_values = [0]
sequence_length = [1]

All tensors are tiny:

inputs shape:          [1, 1, 1]
labels_indices shape:  [1, 2]
labels_values shape:   [1]
sequence_length shape: [1]

However, in my ASan-enabled TensorFlow build, this does not fail with a clean, catchable TensorFlow exception. Instead, the process aborts with an AddressSanitizer bad-free report inside the native CTC loss path:

AddressSanitizer: attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed

This may indicate a memory-safety issue in the tf.raw_ops.CTCLoss CPU implementation. Invalid or unsupported CTC configurations should be rejected deterministically before entering the native loss calculation, preferably with a recoverable Python exception such as InvalidArgumentError.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import tensorflow as tf

inputs = tf.constant([[[-1.0]]], dtype=tf.float32)
labels_indices = tf.constant([[0, 0]], dtype=tf.int64)
labels_values = tf.constant([0], dtype=tf.int32)
sequence_length = tf.constant([1], dtype=tf.int32)

tf.raw_ops.CTCLoss(
    inputs=inputs,
    labels_indices=labels_indices,
    labels_values=labels_values,
    sequence_length=sequence_length,
    preprocess_collapse_repeated=False,
    ctc_merge_repeated=False,
    ignore_longer_outputs_than_inputs=False,
)
```

title: [XLA:GPU] Refactor SM occupancy calculation in GPU dot fusion cost model
body:
[XLA:GPU] Refactor SM occupancy calculation in GPU dot fusion cost model

This is a pure refactor to get down to brass tacks and expose hardware occupancy metrics for future latency-hiding penalties. Currently, the GPU dot fusion cost model underestimates the execution time of heavily memory-bound configurations (e.g., configs with high shared memory usage). It implicitly assumes perfect latency hiding regardless of the physical occupancy on the Streaming Multiprocessor (SM).

By exposing `active_warps_per_sm`, subsequent CLs will be able to evaluate the physical occupancy of a given config. There are a few minor changes that are not affecting any metrics as well.

title: PR #45082: [XLA:GPU] Use packed storage shapes for FP4 XTile operands
body:
PR #45082: [XLA:GPU] Use packed storage shapes for FP4 XTile operands

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45082

📝 Summary of Changes
Update XTile codegen to model packed FP4 scaled-dot operands using their physical storage shape and storage element type. For packed f4E2M1FN operands, XTile now uses i8 storage, divides the packed layout-minor dimension by the number of FP4 elements per byte, adjusts tile offsets for the packed storage coordinate system, and validates that packed tiles use unit stride and byte-aligned offsets. This is the second PR in the decomposition of the larger scaled-dot fix series: https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/44223.

🎯 Justification
FP4 scaled-dot operands are stored packed: two logical f4E2M1FN values live in one byte. After https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/44885, XTile can carry the logical dot element type separately from the tensor storage type. This PR makes the tile and memref storage side consistent with that contract.

This cannot be delayed until Triton lowering because XTile already materializes memref types, tile shapes, slice offsets, and extract geometry before Triton sees the operation. If XTile keeps using logical FP4 shapes at that layer, it can describe incorrect byte storage shapes, tile sizes, and offsets for packed FP4 data. This matters for NVFP4/MXFP4 scaled-dot workloads lowered through Triton, where Triton expects e2m1 operands to be carried as packed i8 storage.

🚀 Kind of Contribution
🐛 Bug Fix, 🧪 Tests

🧪 Unit Tests:
TritonDevicelessTest.RejectsPackedFp4OddMinorOffset verifies that packed FP4 tiles reject byte-unaligned minor offsets.
TritonDevicelessTest.EmitsPackedFp4StorageForEvenMinorOffset verifies that byte-aligned packed FP4 operands use packed i8 memrefs/tensors, storage-coordinate offsets, and dot_scaled i8 storage element types.

Bug

### Have you reproduced the bug with TensorFlow Nightly?

Yes

### Source

source

### TensorFlow version

master (commit 95ffd6ce, 2026-07-16)

### Custom code

No

### OS platform and distribution

N/A - source-level finding, applies to all platforms

### Mobile device

_No response_

### Bazel version

_No response_

### GCC/compiler version

_No response_

### CUDA/cuDNN version

_No response_

### GPU model and memory

_No response_

### Current behavior?

In tensorflow/lite/kernels/rfft2d.cc (Rfft2dHelper, ~line 382) and
tensorflow/lite/kernels/irfft2d.cc (Irfft2dHelper, ~line 330), the FFT
work buffer is allocated with raw `new` BEFORE the temporary tensors
are fetched:

    double** fft_input_output = new double*[fft_height];
    for (int i = 0; i < fft_height; ++i) {
      fft_input_output[i] = new double[fft_width + 2];
    }

    TfLiteTensor* fft_integer_working_area;
    TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK(
        context, GetTemporarySafe(context, node, kFftIntegerWorkingAreaTensor,
                                  &fft_integer_working_area));
    ...
    TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK(context,
                      GetTemporarySafe(context, node, kFftDoubleWorkingAreaTensor,
                                       &fft_double_working_area));

TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK expands to `if (s != kTfLiteOk) return s;`
(lite/core/c/common.h), so if either GetTemporarySafe call fails, the
function returns without reaching the `delete[]` loop at the end of
the helper - leaking fft_height + 1 allocations per failing Eval call.
A long-running process that keeps invoking a failing graph accumulates
the leak.

Expected: the work buffer is released on every path - either fetch the
temporaries before allocating the work buffer, or hold it in RAII
storage (std::vector<std::unique_ptr<double[]>> plus a
std::vector<double*> view; everything downstream takes double**, so
.data() drops in).

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
Not reproducible from a notebook: the leak is on internal error paths -
it triggers only when GetTemporarySafe fails inside Eval, which is not
reachable from well-formed user-level API calls. Found by static
dataflow analysis of master and verified by code inspection: the happy
path frees correctly; only the TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK early-return paths
skip the delete[] loop.

Code pointers (master @ 95ffd6ce):
- tensorflow/lite/kernels/rfft2d.cc: allocation ~382, early returns
  ~390 and ~397, delete[] only at ~419
- tensorflow/lite/kernels/irfft2d.cc: same shape, allocation ~330,
  early return ~337
```

title: Fix CHECK-fail crash in ScatterNd ops when updates rank is too small
body:
Fixes #93680

## Problem

`tf.scatter_nd` aborts the whole process with a fatal `CHECK` failure when the rank of `updates` is smaller than the number of outer dimensions of `indices`:

```python
import tensorflow as tf
indices = tf.constant([[4], [3], [1], [7]])
updates = tf.constant([9, 10, 11, 12])
shape = tf.constant([8])
tf.scatter_nd(tf.expand_dims(indices, axis=-1), updates, shape)
```

```
F0000 tensor_shape.cc:362] Check failed: d < dims() (1 vs. 1)
*** Check failure stack trace: ***
Aborted (core dumped)
```

Reproduced on TF 2.21.0 (pip). The same crash exists in the `TensorScatterUpdate`/`Add`/`Sub`/`Min`/`Max` kernels, e.g. `tf.tensor_scatter_nd_update(tf.ones([8]), tf.zeros([4,1,1], tf.int32), tf.zeros([4]))`.

## Root cause

In `ScatterNdOp::Compute` and `TensorScatterOp::Compute` (`tensorflow/core/kernels/scatter_nd_op.cc`), the outer-dimension matching loop calls `updates.shape().dim_size(i)` for every `i < outer_dims` without first validating that `updates` has at least `outer_dims` dimensions. With `indices` of shape `[4, 1, 1]` (`outer_dims = 2`) and `updates` of rank 1, `dim_size(1)` trips `CHECK(d < dims())` in `TensorShape::dim_size` and aborts.

The deeper kernel path already handles this correctly — `ValidateScatterNdUpdateShape` in `scatter_nd_util.cc` returns `InvalidArgumentError` for `updates_shape.dims() < batch_dim` — but the inline validation in `Compute` crashes before ever reaching it. Graph mode is likewise unaffected (shape inference raises a clean error); only the eager/kernel path aborts.

## Fix

Add a rank guard before the loop in both `Compute` methods so the ops return a regular `InvalidArgumentError` instead of crashing:

```
Updates shape must have rank at least the number of outer dimensions of
indices (2). Found: updates shape=[4], indices shape=[4,1,1]
```

No behavior change for any shapes that pass the guard.

## Tests

Added regression tests in `tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/array_ops/scatter_nd_ops_test.py`:
- `ScatterNdTest.testUpdatesRankSmallerThanIndicesOuterDimsInvalid` (also runs in the inherited `ScatterNdNonAliasingAddTest`, which exercises the already-safe `ScatterNdUpdateOp` path)
- `ScatterNdTensorTest.testUpdatesRankSmallerThanIndicesOuterDimsInvalid` for `tensor_scatter_nd_update`

Both assert `InvalidArgumentError`/`ValueError` is raised instead of a process abort, in graph and eager modes.

title: PR #45595: [XLA:GPU] Support VA remapping of parameter buffer allocations
body:
PR #45595: [XLA:GPU] Support VA remapping of parameter buffer allocations

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45595

## 📝 Summary of Changes

This PR extends command-buffer virtual-address remapping to entry-computation parameter allocations. Parameter buffers remain caller-owned, so each execution aliases their physical memory into stable VA-reservation addresses instead of transferring ownership to the VMM allocator.

- Adds `ExecutionScope::ResolveParameterBuffer`; the base implementation returns the caller buffer, while the VA-remapping implementation installs and returns the stable reservation alias.
- Renames the `PrepareReservation` hook to `Prepare` and makes `ExecuteWithBufferAllocations` accept mutable `BufferAllocations`, allowing addresses to be restored after execution.
- Tracks per-execution parameter aliases with `RecordStepAlias`.
- Releases those aliases after every execution and rewrites remapped entries back to their caller-owned addresses before teardown and result handling. The execution-scope destructor provides cleanup for error paths.
- Adds `AddVaRemappedAllocationForTesting` and a host-only fake VMM allocator to exercise the parameter-remapping path without requiring a GPU.

This PR is stacked on #45567, **[XLA:GPU] Split command buffer VA remapping into its own allocator class**. It is part 1 of 3 splitting the former #45568 implementation into reviewable changes; #45596 adds output-buffer remapping and #45597 adds the `SKIP_PROFILED` mode.

## 🎯 Justification

`SKIP_TEMP` stabilizes only preallocated temporary buffers, but profiled command-buffer update policies also need to stabilize caller-owned parameters whose physical addresses remain constant across executions. Parameter ownership prevents allocating them directly through the command-buffer reservation.

Creating a per-execution alias gives recorded command buffers a stable VA while preserving the caller's original address and ownership. Restoring the original address after execution ensures teardown and result handling never observe a reservation address.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

✨ New Feature

## 📊 Benchmark (for Performance Improvements)

Not applicable as a standalone change. This PR adds parameter-remapping support but does not select it in a production update mode. Performance evaluation belongs to the final `SKIP_PROFILED` policy in #45597.

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

- Added host-only `gpu_executable_va_remap_allocator_test.cc` coverage using a fake VMM allocator.
- Verifies that a caller-owned parameter receives the same stable reservation address across executions.
- Verifies persistent allocation-index handling, post-execution restoration to the caller address, and release of each per-execution mapping.
- Covers cleanup behavior without requiring a GPU.

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

No standalone execution test is added because no production update mode selects parameter allocations in this PR. End-to-end selection and execution coverage is provided by the stacked `SKIP_PROFILED` change in #45597.

Allow command buffer VA remapping to give stable reservation addresses
to entry-computation-parameter allocations. Parameter buffers are owned
by the caller, so they are aliased into the VA reservation with Map()
each execution instead of being allocated through it:

- GpuExecutableBufferAllocator::ExecutionScope gains a
  ResolveParameterBuffer hook (base returns the caller buffer), and
  ExecuteWithBufferAllocations now takes a mutable BufferAllocations so
  subclasses can rewrite entries after execution. The Prepare hook is
  renamed from PrepareReservation.
- GpuExecutableVaRemapAllocator records each installed alias

  rewrites the remapped BufferAllocations entries back to the
  caller-owned addresses so TearDown and result handling never see
  reservation addresses (ReleaseStepAliases; the scope destructor is a
  safety net for error paths).
- No production update mode selects parameter allocations yet
  (SKIP_TEMP remaps only preallocated temp buffers); the
  AddVaRemappedAllocationForTesting seam plus a host-only fake VMM
  allocator (gpu_executable_va_remap_allocator_test.cc) exercise the
  new path: stable reservation address across executions, persistent
  allocation indices, post-execution rewrite, and mapping release.

title: Validate vocab_size against dataset cardinality in table_from_dataset
body:
Fixes #113162

## Problem
`table_from_dataset` (and its wrapper `index_table_from_dataset`) only
validated that `vocab_size >= 1`, with no upper-bound check. Passing an
oversized `vocab_size` reached the C++ table initializer and aborted
the entire process with `std::bad_alloc` instead of raising a
recoverable Python exception.

## Fix
Added a check that cross-references `vocab_size` against the dataset's
known static cardinality (when determinable) and raises
`InvalidArgumentError` before the value reaches the C++ layer.

## Testing
Added two regression tests covering both `table_from_dataset` and
`index_table_from_dataset` with an oversized `vocab_size`. Ran the full
existing test file locally — 10 passed, 1 skipped (unrelated), no
regressions.

title: [XLA:GPU] Rewrite seeded and live carry add scans to CUB device scans.
body:
[XLA:GPU] Rewrite seeded and live carry add scans to CUB device scans.

The CUB scan rewriter only matched forward add scans with an all zero
scalar init and a dead final carry; everything else fell through to
the sequential while loop expansion, and the reverse support already
plumbed to the kernel was unreachable. By associativity, a seeded
inclusive add scan is the unseeded scan plus the broadcast seed, and
its final carry is the boundary output element. Rewrite non zero
inits as one elementwise add of the broadcast init to the CUB result,
feed live final carry users a slice of the output at the last scanned
position, and match reverse scans. With this, scans that the SPMD
partitioner shards on their scan dimension lower to per shard CUB
scans instead of while loops.

body:
Properly move iota_ (`std::move(other.iota_)`) and null out other.array_ (`std::exchange(other.array_, nullptr)`) inside TileAssignment move constructor and move assignment operator.

When `HloSharding` is moved around and assigned over during XLA passes such as `XPrecisionRewriter` (`ReplaceInstruction`), leaving `other.array_` non-null inside the moved-from `TileAssignment` while moving out `shared_array_` causes dangling pointers and aliased deallocations upon subsequent array access or assignment. Furthermore, copying `iota_` (`std::optional<IotaTileAssignment>`) instead of moving it creates duplicate internal allocations.

Using `std::move` and `std::exchange` ensures clean transfer of pointer ownership and prevents `free(): invalid pointer` crashes.

title: [IFRT] Copy serialized Cord to std::string during deserialization to avoid ASan buffer overflow
body:
[IFRT] Copy serialized Cord to std::string during deserialization to avoid ASan buffer overflow

MLIR Lexer (used by the text/assembly parser) assumes the input buffer is null-terminated.
When parsing text-based StableHLO during deserialization (e.g. on invalid input in tests), `deserializePortableArtifact` receives a non-null-terminated `absl::string_view` from `absl::Cord::Flatten()`.
If an identifier ends exactly at the buffer boundary, the lexer reads past the end of the buffer, causing an ASan `stack-buffer-overflow`.

To fix this safely, we copy the serialized data to a `std::string` to guarantee null-termination before passing it to MLIR parsing. Since this only happens during program deserialization (non-hot path), the performance impact is expected to be low, but we will need to do a follow-up if the extra cost turns out to be too high.

Modify CommonPjRtClient to use ExecuteArgHold for execution arguments to support undonatable buffers.

Implement CopyRawToHostFuture and AcquireExternalReference for UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer

This change adds the following implementations to UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer:

#### CopyRawToHostFuture: 
Performs an asynchronous device-to-host data transfer and respects definition event dependencies. Ensures the underlying PjRtRawBuffer remains valid until the copy operation completes by holding a reference.

#### AcquireExternalReference: 
Provides a PjRtBuffer::ExternalReference object. The returned reference maintains a refcount on the underlying PjRtRawBuffer, keeping the device memory valid for the lifetime of the reference. This operation does not block on definition events.

title: Fix tf.sigmoid on bfloat16 CPU non-monotonicity and rounding issues
body:
# Fix non-monotonicity and incorrect rounding of tf.sigmoid on bfloat16 CPU

Fixes #123104

### Problem
When evaluating `tf.sigmoid` (logistic function) on `bfloat16` CPU inputs in eager/graph mode, the results are non-monotonic and not correctly rounded (unlike in XLA, which returns correctly rounded values). 

For example:
* `sigmoid(5.5)` yields `0.99609375`
* `sigmoid(5.75)` yields `0.9921875` (a smaller output for a larger input, violating monotonicity).

This behavior stems from the default template implementation of Eigen's `scalar_logistic_op` evaluated directly in `bfloat16` precision. Because `bfloat16` has only 7 mantissa bits, performing three consecutive low-precision operations (`exp(x)`, then `1 + exp(x)`, and finally `exp(x) / (1 + exp(x))`) accumulates significant rounding errors.

### Solution
This PR fixes the issue by specializing `scalar_logistic_op<Eigen::bfloat16>` and its corresponding `functor_traits` in `tensorflow/core/kernels/cwise_ops.h`:
1. It casts `bfloat16` inputs to `float32` (`float`), performs the sigmoid computation in high-precision, and casts the result back to `bfloat16` once at the very end.
2. It sets `PacketAccess` to `false` for `Eigen::bfloat16` in `functor_traits` to disable SIMD packet vectorization on CPU, ensuring computations route correctly through the high-precision scalar specialization.

This ensures a maximum of one rounding operation, guaranteeing correct rounding and strict monotonicity.

---

### Changes

#### 1. Core Kernels
* **`tensorflow/core/kernels/cwise_ops.h`**:
  * Specialized `scalar_logistic_op<Eigen::bfloat16>` to calculate sigmoid values in `float` precision.
  * Specialized `functor_traits<scalar_logistic_op<Eigen::bfloat16>>` to set `PacketAccess = false`.

#### 2. Tests
* **`tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/math_ops/cwise_ops_unary_test.py`**:
  * Added `math_ops.sigmoid` to basic `bfloat16` tests (`testBFloat16Basic`).
  * Added `testBFloat16SigmoidMonotonicityAndRounding` to verify `sigmoid` correctness and monotonicity near the rounding threshold (specifically testing inputs `5.5`, `5.75`, `6.0`, and `6.25`).

---

### Verification
The changes were verified using the newly added test case `testBFloat16SigmoidMonotonicityAndRounding` which specifically tests:
* **Correct Rounding**:
  * `sigmoid(5.5)` $\rightarrow$ `0.99609375` (exact `0.995929...`)
  * `sigmoid(5.75)` $\rightarrow$ `0.99609375` (exact `0.996817...`)
  * `sigmoid(6.0)` $\rightarrow$ `0.99609375` (exact `0.997527...`)
  * `sigmoid(6.25)` $\rightarrow$ `1.0` (exact `0.998075...`)
* **Strict Monotonicity**: Asserts that `y_val[i] <= y_val[i+1]` across the tested range.

title: Fix Round returning zeros for integer tensors (#74789)
body:
### Problem

`tf.raw_ops.Round` (and any op using `functor::round`) returns all zeros for integer tensors instead of the input values:

```python
>>> tf.raw_ops.Round(x=tf.constant([-2, -1, 1, 2, 3], dtype=tf.int32))
<tf.Tensor: shape=(5,), dtype=int32, numpy=array([0, 0, 0, 0, 0])>  # expected [-2, -1, 1, 2, 3]
```

This is a regression: TF 2.16 returned the input unchanged; TF 2.17+ returns zeros.

Fixes #74789

### Root cause

`scalar_round_half_to_even_op<Scalar, IsInteger, HasRint>` in `tensorflow/core/kernels/cwise_ops.h` has an integer specialization that was tightened to `<Scalar, true, /*HasRint=*/false>` when the `HasRint` template parameter was introduced. For integer types where `packet_traits<Scalar>::HasRound == true`, the type instantiates as `<Scalar, true, true>`, no longer matches the identity specialization, and falls through to the floating-point primary template — producing zeros.

### Fix

Relax the integer specialization to `<Scalar, true, HasRint>` so integer rounding is the identity for any value of `HasRint`, restoring the pre-regression behavior. The float `rint` path (`<Scalar, false, true>`) is untouched and there is no partial-ordering ambiguity.

### Testing

Adds `UnaryOpTest.testRoundIntIsIdentity` in `cwise_ops_unary_test.py`, asserting the kernel is the identity for `int32`/`int64`. It calls `gen_math_ops.round` directly, because `math_ops.round` short-circuits integer dtypes in Python and would not exercise the kernel (which is why existing coverage missed the regression).

CC @mihaimaruseac

PR #44560: [ROCm][Triton] All gather thunk dispatch (PR2/4)

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/44560

📝 Summary of Changes
This PR is the second in a series of four.

PR 1/4: https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/44559   
PR 2/4: https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/44560   <--- This PR
PR 3/4: https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/44562

Stack:

1. #45419 — reclaim tests, PA accounting, and typed overlap filters

📝 Summary of Changes

Mapped allocation reuse and creation previously duplicated most of their logic for two address layouts. The paths could drift in budget handling, pending reclamation, and record installation despite implementing the same lifecycle. title: PR #45567: [XLA:GPU] Split command buffer VA remapping into its own allocator class
body:
PR #45567: [XLA:GPU] Split command buffer VA remapping into its own allocator class

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45567

## 📝 Summary of Changes

This PR separates the command-buffer virtual-address remapping implementation from `GpuExecutableBufferAllocator` into a dedicated `GpuExecutableVaRemapAllocator` subclass. It is a structural refactor of the existing `SKIP_TEMP` behavior; no functional change is intended.

- `GpuExecutableBufferAllocator` is now the common base implementation for allocation resolution and the `ALWAYS_UPDATE` policy. It also remains the runtime fallback for `SKIP_TEMP` when VA remapping is unavailable.
- `ExecutionScope` is now polymorphic and is returned as `std::unique_ptr<ExecutionScope>`. Protected hooks such as `PrepareReservation` and `AllocateTransientBuffer` provide the extension points needed by address-policy-specific subclasses.
- The new `GpuExecutableVaRemapAllocator` owns the `SKIP_TEMP` implementation:
  - per-executor remapping state and synchronization;
  - deterministic VA reservation sizing and layout;
  - VMM-backed allocation of command-buffer-referenced temporary buffers;
  - persistent allocation indices combining constants with VA-remapped temporary allocations; and
  - synchronization of pending VMM operations during allocator teardown.
- `GpuExecutableBufferAllocator::Create` selects the base allocator for `ALWAYS_UPDATE` and the VA-remapping subclass for `SKIP_TEMP`.
- GPU executable and PJRT call sites now use the factory and pointer-owned execution scopes.
- The BUILD target includes the new source/header pair and retains the direct dependencies required by both implementations.
- VMM test logging now enables both allocator translation units so existing assertions continue to observe the VA-reservation messages after the code move.

This PR is stacked on #45130, **[XLA:GPU] Update command buffers when allocation policy changes**. The follow-up policy is implemented separately in #45568.

## 🎯 Justification

The base allocator previously mixed general buffer-allocation mechanics with one specific VMM address-stability policy. Splitting those responsibilities makes the default path easier to reason about and gives additional update policies a narrow place to implement reservation, allocation, and execution behavior without further expanding the base class.

This cleanup is primarily preparation for profiled command-buffer allocation policies. Existing GPU command-buffer workloads should retain the same `ALWAYS_UPDATE` and `SKIP_TEMP` behavior.

♻️ Cleanup

## 📊 Benchmark (for Performance Improvements)

Not applicable. This is a behavior-preserving refactor and makes no performance claim.

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

- Updated `GpuExecutableTest.CommandBufferAllocationPolicy` to construct allocators through the new factory and exercise the pointer-owned `ExecutionScope`.
- Existing assertions continue to cover the persistent-allocation sets for `ALWAYS_UPDATE` and `SKIP_TEMP`, including the non-VMM fallback path.

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

- Existing `VmmTest` command-buffer tests continue to cover the two-GEMM `SKIP_TEMP` path, VA reservation reuse, and fallback when the configured allocator does not provide VMM remapping.
- `ScopedBufferAllocatorVLog` now captures logs from `gpu_executable_va_remap_allocator.cc`, preserving the execution-test assertions whose log statements moved with the implementation.

### Current behavior?

`tf.reduce_mean` returns an inaccurate result for a constant float16 tensor containing large values. As a consequence, `tf.math.reduce_std` returns a nonzero standard deviation even though all input elements are identical.
For a constant tensor where every element equals `10000.0`, the expected mean is exactly `10000.0` and the standard deviation should be exactly `0.0`. However, TensorFlow computes a mean of approximately `9.99e+03 (i.e., 9992)`, which subsequently causes `tf.math.reduce_std` to return `8.0`.
Since all elements in the input tensor have the same value, the standard deviation is expected to be exactly 0.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf 
x_np = np.array( 
    [ 
        [10000.0, 10000.0], 
        [10000.0, 10000.0], 
        [10000.0, 10000.0], 
    ], 
    dtype=np.float16, 
) 
x = tf.constant(x_np, dtype=tf.float16)
mean = tf.reduce_mean(x) 
std = tf.math.reduce_std(x) 
print("TensorFlow mean:", mean) 
print("TensorFlow std :", std) 
print("NumPy mean:", np.mean(x_np, dtype=np.float16))
print("NumPy std :", np.std(x_np, dtype=np.float16))
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
TensorFlow mean: tf.Tensor(9.99e+03, shape=(), dtype=float16)
TensorFlow std : tf.Tensor(8.0, shape=(), dtype=float16)
NumPy mean: 1e+04
NumPy std : 0.0
```

title: [XLA:GPU] Refactor DotMerger to use DotOperandDims and ShapeTracker.
body:
[XLA:GPU] Refactor DotMerger to use DotOperandDims and ShapeTracker.

This change enhances the capabilities of the DotMerger pass. Instead of relying on specific patterns like DotDecomposer's normal form, the new implementation uses `DotOperandDims` to track and categorize dimensions (Batch, Contracting, NonContracting) and `ShapeTracker` to generate the necessary transformation instructions (transpose, reshape, bitcast) to align operand shapes for merging.

Key improvements include:
-   Support for merging dots with different layouts on the shared or concatenated operands.
-   Ability to handle dots with arbitrary batch, contracting, and non-contracting dimension orders.
-   Merging of dots even when the non-shared operands have multiple non-contracting dimensions.
-   Improved handling of dependencies by merging only mutually unreachable dots within an equivalence class.
-   Simplification of consumer chains (transposes, reshapes, bitcasts) after the merged dot's output is sliced.

The equivalence classes are now built based on the shared operand's source instruction and the categorized dimensions at that source, allowing for more flexible grouping. The merging process involves transforming the operands to a common shape/layout before concatenation and then creating a single large dot. The results are then sliced and potentially transformed back to match the original dot outputs.

title: fix complex dtype byte-swap overrun in ByteSwapBuffer

labels.name: comp:core
labels.description: issues related to core part of tensorflow

body:
ByteSwapBuffer computes the number of components to swap, then ByteSwapArray walks that many words in place. On the num_of_elem == -1 path the count comes from the byte size: array_len = size / bytes_per_elem, where bytes_per_elem is the 4- or 8-byte component size, so array_len already counts every component in the buffer. For DT_COMPLEX64/DT_COMPLEX128 the code then does array_len *= 2, so ByteSwapArray swaps twice as many words as the buffer holds and reads/writes size bytes past the end. This path is taken when a cross-endian SavedModel or GraphDef is loaded on a big-endian host (ByteSwapTensorContentInNode, and the public ByteSwapTensorProto), where the dtype and tensor_content length come straight from the file, so a complex Const overruns the copy buffer.

Only double the count on the num_of_elem branch, where it is an element count that has to become a component count; the size-derived branch is already the component count. The sibling ByteSwapTensor path (which passes t->NumElements()) confirms the intended arithmetic. Added a regression test that runs ByteSwapTensorProto over both complex dtypes and checks the content round-trips without overrunning.

title: Add rotate expander pass for kRotate.

Add rotate expander pass for kRotate.

Extend the HLO optimization pipeline with an expander for `HloOpcode::kRotate`, allowing compiler pipelines to expand them into known ops when target backends do not provide native rotate lowering.

Specifically, this commit introduces:
* **RotateExpander (`rotate_expander.h/cc`)**: Add an `OpExpanderPass` that decomposes `kRotate` instructions into a sequence of `kSlice` and `kConcatenate` operations (`concat(slice(shift:), slice(0:shift))`) along each rotated dimension for backends without native rotation support.

title: Add algebraic simplification logic for kRotate.

Extend the HLO optimization pipeline with algebraic simplifications for `HloOpcode::kRotate`, allowing compiler pipelines to simplify rotations.

Specifically, this commit introduces:
* **AlgebraicSimplifier (`algebraic_simplifier.cc`)**: Add simplification rules for `kRotate` instructions

title: Remove incorrect TF_Involution trait from tf.Reciprocal
body:
## Summary

The MLIR TF dialect marks `tf.Reciprocal` with the `TF_Involution` trait, whose fold hook rewrites `Reciprocal(Reciprocal(x))` to `x`. Reciprocal is not an exact involution:

- In floating point, `1 / (1 / x)` does not round-trip to `x` because the inner reciprocal is already rounded (`reciprocal(reciprocal(7.0)) = 6.9999995`).
- For integer types, `1 / x` truncates to zero for `|x| > 1`, so `reciprocal(reciprocal(3))` is `0`, not `3`.

The fold silently changes computed results wherever the TF MLIR canonicalization pipeline runs. This is the MLIR counterpart of #123195, which fixed the same root cause (#119429) in Grappler's `RemoveInvolution` stage.

## Changes

- **`tf_generated_ops.td` / `tf_ops.td`** — drop `TF_Involution` from `TF_ReciprocalOp`. Per the generated file's header, the modified definition moves to `tf_ops.td`, with a comment documenting why the trait is absent. The remaining `TF_Involution` ops (`Conj`, `Invert`, `LogicalNot`, `Neg`) are all exact involutions.
- **`tests/tf_trait_folds.mlir`, `tests/canonicalize.mlir`** — the double/triple Reciprocal tests now assert the ops are preserved instead of folding to the argument.

title: The TFLite REVERSE_SEQUENCE operator incorrectly bounds-checked its `seq_lengths` parameter. The validation loop iterated over the rank of the tensor (`NumDimensions`) instead of the number of elements (`NumElements`), meaning only the first sequence length was validated. Furthermore, it failed to check for negative values. An attacker could supply an adversarial `.tflite` model with negative or extremely large values in the unvalidated elements of `seq_lengths`, leading to an arbitrary heap out-of-bounds write when calculating destination offsets for a `memcpy` operation in the reference implementation.
body:
The TFLite REVERSE_SEQUENCE operator incorrectly bounds-checked its `seq_lengths` parameter. The validation loop iterated over the rank of the tensor (`NumDimensions`) instead of the number of elements (`NumElements`), meaning only the first sequence length was validated. Furthermore, it failed to check for negative values. An attacker could supply an adversarial `.tflite` model with negative or extremely large values in the unvalidated elements of `seq_lengths`, leading to an arbitrary heap out-of-bounds write when calculating destination offsets for a `memcpy` operation in the reference implementation.

This commit fixes the issue by updating the validation loop to iterate over all elements using `NumElements(seq_lengths_tensor)`. It also adds a lower bound check to ensure all `seq_lengths` elements are non-negative, fully ensuring they remain within the valid range `[0, seq_size]`.

Also adds unit tests (`InvalidSeqLengthsNegative` and `InvalidSeqLengthsTooLarge`) to `reverse_sequence_test.cc`, removes an unused `tensor.h` include from `reverse_sequence.cc`, and adds direct header includes (`gmock.h`, `c_api_types.h`) along with the required `BUILD` dependency (`//third_party/tensorflow/lite/core/c:c_api_types`) to `reverse_sequence_test.cc` to satisfy static analysis checks.

body:
### Issue type

### OS platform and distribution

### Mobile device

!python --version

### Bazel version

_No response_

### GCC/compiler version

_No response_

### CUDA/cuDNN version

_No response_

### GPU model and memory

T4 GPU

### Current behavior?

When dynamically instantiating and executing pipelines using `tf.data.Dataset.from_generator` on a GPU-enabled runtime, a progressive host memory (RSS) leak occurs. 

Even after manually deleting the dataset references and forcing Python garbage collection (`gc.collect()`), the host resident memory steadily climbs (e.g., leaking ~128 MB over 500 minor iterations on a 1000x1000 float32 tensor). The leak resides entirely on the Host (CPU) RAM rather than GPU VRAM (which remains clean at 0.00 MB growth). 

This indicates that background C++ coordinating threads or graph execution nodes associated with the `GeneratorDataset` fail to tear down and release their heap memory.

What I expected to happen:
Once `del dataset` and `gc.collect()` are executed, all associated host-side C++ coordinator resources, thread states, and execution context memory should be fully released. The Host RAM growth after the benchmark run should return to or near 0.00 MB.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
#!/usr/bin/env python3


import argparse
import gc
import logging
import os
import sys
import time

# Suppress standard TensorFlow initialization spam
os.environ["TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL"] = "3"
# ENABLE GPU: Ensure CUDA devices are visible
if "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES" in os.environ:
    del os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"]

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s",
    handlers=[logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)]
)

try:
    import psutil
except ImportError:
    logging.error("The 'psutil' library is required to run this benchmark. Install with: pip install psutil")
    sys.exit(1)

try:
    import tensorflow as tf
except ImportError:
    logging.error("TensorFlow is not installed in the current environment.")
    sys.exit(1)


# Setup GPU memory growth to prevent TF from occupying 100% VRAM instantly
gpus = tf.config.list_physical_devices('GPU')
if gpus:
    try:
        for gpu in gpus:
            tf.config.experimental.set_memory_growth(gpu, True)
        logging.info(f"GPU detected and configured with dynamic memory growth. Count: {len(gpus)}")
    except RuntimeError as e:
        # Memory growth must be set before GPUs have been initialized
        logging.warning(f"Could not set GPU memory growth: {e}")
else:
    logging.warning("No GPU detected. Running on CPU instead.")


class GPUMemoryLeakBenchmark:
    def __init__(self, iterations: int, dim: int):
        self.iterations = iterations
        self.dim = dim
        self.process = psutil.Process(os.getpid())
        self.has_gpu = len(tf.config.list_physical_devices('GPU')) > 0
        
    def _get_host_rss(self) -> float:
        """Returns Host Resident Set Size (physical memory) in Megabytes."""
        return self.process.memory_info().rss / (1024 * 1024)

    def _get_gpu_vram(self) -> float:
        """Returns Active GPU VRAM used by TensorFlow in Megabytes (if GPU is present)."""
        if self.has_gpu:
            try:
                # Returns dict with 'current' and 'peak' in bytes
                mem_info = tf.config.experimental.get_memory_info('GPU:0')
                return mem_info['current'] / (1024 * 1024)
            except Exception:
                return 0.0
        return 0.0

    def dummy_generator(self):
        # We explicitly generate the tensor on the default device context
        yield tf.random.normal((self.dim, self.dim))

    def execute(self) -> dict:
        logging.info(f"Initializing Benchmark | TF Version: {tf.__version__}")
        logging.info(f"Parameters | Iterations: {self.iterations} | Tensor Dimensions: {self.dim}x{self.dim}")
        
        # Settle memory baseline
        gc.collect()
        tf.keras.backend.clear_session()
        time.sleep(1.0)
        
        initial_rss = self._get_host_rss()
        initial_vram = self._get_gpu_vram()
        
        logging.info(f"Baseline Host RAM (RSS): {initial_rss:.2f} MB")
        if self.has_gpu:
            logging.info(f"Baseline GPU VRAM: {initial_vram:.2f} MB")
        
        step_interval = max(1, self.iterations // 5)
        
        for step in range(1, self.iterations + 1):
            # Instantiate generator context
            dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_generator(
                self.dummy_generator,
                output_signature=tf.TensorSpec(shape=(self.dim, self.dim), dtype=tf.float32)
            )
            
            # Consume 1 element to trigger graph compilation, execution, and GPU heap allocation
            for _ in dataset.take(1):
                pass
            
            # Force target deallocation
            del dataset
            
            # Periodically force python garbage collection
            if step % 10 == 0:
                gc.collect()
                
            # Log current metrics at standardized milestones
            if step % step_interval == 0 or step == self.iterations:
                current_rss = self._get_host_rss()
                current_vram = self._get_gpu_vram()
                delta_rss = current_rss - initial_rss
                delta_vram = current_vram - initial_vram
                
                vram_str = f" | VRAM: {current_vram:7.2f} MB (Growth: +{delta_vram:6.2f} MB)" if self.has_gpu else ""
                logging.info(
                    f"Iteration {step:5d}/{self.iterations} | "
                    f"Host RAM: {current_rss:7.2f} MB (Growth: +{delta_rss:6.2f} MB)" + vram_str
                )

        # Final memory cleanup run
        gc.collect()
        tf.keras.backend.clear_session()
        time.sleep(1.0)
        
        final_rss = self._get_host_rss()
        final_vram = self._get_gpu_vram()
        
        total_host_leak = final_rss - initial_rss
        total_vram_leak = final_vram - initial_vram
        
        return {
            "initial_rss": initial_rss,
            "final_rss": final_rss,
            "total_host_leak": total_host_leak,
            "initial_vram": initial_vram,
            "final_vram": final_vram,
            "total_vram_leak": total_vram_leak,
            "leak_detected": (total_host_leak > 15.0 or total_vram_leak > 15.0)
        }


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="TF Generator Memory Leak GPU Check Suite")
    parser.add_argument("--iterations", type=int, default=500, help="Number of benchmark iterations")
    parser.add_argument("--dim", type=int, default=1000, help="Dimension of square tensor used in test")
    
    # parse_known_args safely ignores Colab/Jupyter connection flags like '-f'.
    args, unknown = parser.parse_known_args()

    benchmark = GPUMemoryLeakBenchmark(iterations=args.iterations, dim=args.dim)
    results = benchmark.execute()
    
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("                 BENCHMARK RESULT (GPU ENABLED)")
    print("="*60)
    print(f"Initial Host RAM (RSS): {results['initial_rss']:.2f} MB")
    print(f"Final Host RAM (RSS):   {results['final_rss']:.2f} MB")
    print(f"Net Host RAM Leak:      {results['total_host_leak']:.2f} MB")
    print("-" * 60)
    if benchmark.has_gpu:
        print(f"Initial GPU VRAM:       {results['initial_vram']:.2f} MB")
        print(f"Final GPU VRAM:         {results['final_vram']:.2f} MB")
        print(f"Net GPU VRAM Leak:      {results['total_vram_leak']:.2f} MB")
        print("-" * 60)
    
    if results["leak_detected"]:
        print("STATUS: FAILED (Confirmed Progressive Memory Leak)")
        print("Impact: Unmanaged resources (CPU or GPU) are not freed dynamically.")
        if "ipykernel" not in sys.modules:
            sys.exit(1)
    else:
        print("STATUS: PASSED (Stable Memory Utilization Profile)")
        if "ipykernel" not in sys.modules:
            sys.exit(0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

title: PR #44403: [XLA:CPU] onednn_threadpool: cap num_workers at n in parallel_for
body:
PR #44403: [XLA:CPU] onednn_threadpool: cap num_workers at n in parallel_for

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/44403

📝 Summary of Changes
`OneDnnThreadPool::parallel_for` (xla/backends/cpu/runtime/onednn/onednn_threadpool.h)  was passing `thread_pool_- NumThreads()` as `num_workers` regardless of `n`. Before   #42581, `Worker::Parallelize` had an entry-point clamp (`num_workers = std::min(num_work_items, num_workers)`) that silently fixed this up. #42581 replaced that clamp with a branch that triggers when `num_workers > num_work_items`:

  ```cpp
  if (num_workers > num_work_items) {
    num_partitions = ceil(num_work_items / 8);
    num_workers   = std::min(num_workers, num_partitions);
  }
  ```

  For oneDNN's small-n dispatches (reorders, packing, eltwise/softmax tiles), this collapses parallelism to ceil(n/8) cores. 
  eg: On a 56-thread host, n = 20 drops from 20 active cores to 3; n <= 8 falls through to a fully serial fallback. Multiplied across the many small primitives, this causes significant regression across multiple models when built with `build_with_onednn_async=true` and `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_cpu_experimental_onednn_custom_call=true`

  Fix
  Cap num_workers at n at the caller, matching the pattern already used in xla/backends/cpu/runtime/kernel.cc and xla/backends/cpu/runtime/convolution_lib.h: 
  ```cpp
  const size_t num_workers = std::min<size_t>(static_cast<size_t>(n),
                                              thread_pool_->NumThreads());
  ```

  With num_workers <= num_work_items, the call takes the else branch (num_partitions = num_workers) and behaves like pre-#42581. For n >= NumThreads(), the cap is a no-op and the heap/cacheline win from #42581 is fully preserved.


🎯 Justification
It fixes the significant regression (25%-60%) across multiple models run on CPU with onednn

title: [PjRt-IFRT] Reject XLA HloShardingV3 (NamedSharding) format in IFRT `HloShardingSerDes` serialization
body:
[PjRt-IFRT] Reject XLA HloShardingV3 (NamedSharding) format in IFRT `HloShardingSerDes` serialization

XLA `HloShardingV3` (NamedSharding) format is currently not version compatible across IFRT SerDes versions as the version compatibility contract has not been established around `HloShardingV3`, and `HloShardingV3` is intended to be used within the local XLA compiler. Allowing `HloShardingSerDes` to serialize `HloShardingV3` format can cause potential compatibility errors when communicating across different binary versions or using persistent artifacts such as model exports.

This change updates `HloShardingSerDes::Serialize` to explicitly reject `HloSharding` containing `HloShardingV3` format, returning an `InvalidArgumentError`.

title: [XLA:CPU] Optimize while loop dead parameter removal using DynamicBitset.
body:
[XLA:CPU] Optimize while loop dead parameter removal using DynamicBitset.

Replaces the heap-allocating InputIndicesSet and other index sets in TryRemoveDeadWhileParams with a custom, auto-resizing DynamicBitset using inlined storage. This avoids expensive heap allocations and speeds up merges.

Microbenchmark comparison (DynamicBitset vs absl::flat_hash_set<int64_t>):
- Add/32: ~24x faster (119 ns vs 2820 ns)
- Contains/32: ~7x faster (76.6 ns vs 553 ns)
- Merge/32: ~300x faster (9.72 ns vs 3095 ns)
For larger sets (512 elements, exceeding inline capacity):
- Add/512: ~17x faster (2076 ns vs 35795 ns)
- Contains/512: ~7x faster (1274 ns vs 8982 ns)
- Merge/512: ~160x faster (254 ns vs 42920 ns)

title: [XLA:BF16_PROP] Do not propagate precision across element-type-converting bitcasts and protect bitcast operands
body:
[XLA:BF16_PROP] Do not propagate precision across element-type-converting bitcasts and protect bitcast operands

Fixes an infinite loop in BFloat16Propagation::ResolveInconsistencyOfAliasingBuffersHelper across bitcast instructions with mismatched input/output element types (e.g. bf16 <-> f32 or u32 <-> f32). Specifically:
- BFloat16Propagation::ShouldKeepPrecisionUnchanged returns true for HloOpcode::kBitcast when the input element type differs from the output element type.
- AllUsersConsumeBF16 returns true when checking a user instruction that is an HloOpcode::kBitcast whose operand expects BF16.
- Ensure only F32 values (value->shape().element_type() == F32) are inserted into values_that_must_be_kept_as_f32_ in DetermineInstructionPrecision and AdjustCalledComputationRoot, preventing F32 bitcast roots from marking aliased native BF16 operands as requiring F32.

title: PR #45130: [XLA:GPU] Trigger command buffers update when persistent allocations set changed.
body:
PR #45130: [XLA:GPU] Trigger command buffers update when persistent allocations set changed.

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45130

For command buffer run, add the required processing for allowing `persistent_alloc_indices` to transition only from absent to present across execution steps and must remain unchanged once present. 

We may require this transition because the chosen of buffer allocations whose address are in `persistent_alloc_indices` might not be available from the first step, e.g, if persistent allocations are only available after several steps of profiling.  So we need to make sure that command buffer is correctly updated when `persistent_alloc_indices` is changed across steps. 


📝 Summary of Changes

- Document that `persistent_alloc_indices` may transition only from absent to
  present across execution steps and must remain unchanged once present.
- Track only whether persistent-allocation information was valid when each
  executor's command buffer was recorded, avoiding an owned vector copy and
  repeated value comparisons.
- Force a full command-buffer update in `CommandBufferThunk::Initialize` when
  persistent allocation information first becomes valid.
- In `ExecuteOnStream`, recover from a recorded/current information-validity
  mismatch by fully updating the command buffer. This covers a
  profiling-skipped update and interleaving with an older execution initialized
  before policy activation.
- Use the public `ShapedSlice` header and its direct BUILD dependency.

🎯 Justification

The persistent allocation policy controls which recorded addresses a command
buffer can safely retain. When the policy first becomes available, an
allocation-filtered update can skip a command whose allocations are now all
persistent, leaving stale addresses in the command buffer. A full update fixes
that transition.

Although the policy transition is logically one-way, executions initialized on
opposite sides of it can interleave on the shared per-executor command buffer.
An Execute-time validity check therefore forces a full update for either
recorded/current mismatch without comparing policy vectors on every step.

🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

📊 Benchmark (for Performance Improvements)

N/A. This is a correctness fix.

🧪 Unit Tests:

Extended `PersistentAllocIndicesBecomingAvailableTriggersUpdate` to verify:

- absent-to-present activation during Initialize triggers exactly one update;
- Execute recovers when the initialization update was skipped;
- an older absent-policy execution and the following present-policy execution
  each restore the correct recorded addresses when they interleave.

Also ran `GpuExecutableTest.CommandBufferAllocationPolicy`.

🧪 Execution Tests:

Ran the focused command-buffer regression and allocation-policy test with
Bazel. All seven configured GPU architecture variants of
`command_buffer_thunk_test` passed, and `gpu_executable_test` passed.

title: Support kRotate in SPMD partitioning and cross-device collective lowering.
body:
Support kRotate in SPMD partitioning and cross-device collective lowering.

Extend the SPMD partitioner (`SpmdPartitioningVisitor`) to natively partition first-class `HloOpcode::kRotate` (`HloRotateInstruction`) operations across sharded tensor dimensions, lowering sharded rotations into cross-device collective right-rotate custom calls (`RotateRight`).

Specifically, this commit introduces:
* **Pattern Matching & Utilities (`spmd_partitioner_util.h/cc`)**:
  - Generalize `FindRotateRightPattern` to return `std::optional<RotateRightPatternMatch>` containing `{dim, amount, rotate_dim_idx}`, enabling it to match both sharded first-class `HloRotateInstruction` operations and the traditional `kConcatenate` of slices pattern.
  - Add `PopRotateDimension` helper to pop a handled `(dimension, shift)` pair in-place from a multi-dimensional `HloRotateInstruction`. When all rotate dimensions are popped, it removes the instruction and replaces uses with `operand(0)`.
* **SPMD Partitioner (`spmd_partitioner.cc`)**:
  - Update `PartitionComputation` to loop over `FindRotateRightPattern(hlo)` matches, emitting `CreateCustomCallSPMDInternal_RotateRight` collective operations along sharded dimensions.
  - Use `PopRotateDimension` when matching `kRotate` (`rotate_dim_idx >= 0`) so multi-dimensional rotations can peel off sharded dimensions one by one while preserving any remaining unpartitioned rotations.
* **Testing**: Add unit tests in `SpmdPartitioningTest` and `SPMDPartitionerUtilTest` covering single- and multi-dimensional sharded `kRotate` partitioning and pattern matching.

title: Add algebraic simplification, rotate expander, and constant folding passes for kRotate.
body:
Add algebraic simplification, rotate expander, and constant folding passes for kRotate.

Extend the HLO optimization pipeline with passes and simplifications for `HloOpcode::kRotate`, allowing compiler pipelines to simplify rotations, evaluate them at compile time, and expand them when target backends do not provide native rotate lowering.

Specifically, this commit introduces:
* **RotateExpander (`rotate_expander.h/cc`)**: Add an `OpExpanderPass` that decomposes `kRotate` instructions into a sequence of `kSlice` and `kConcatenate` operations (`concat(slice(shift:), slice(0:shift))`) along each rotated dimension for backends without native rotation support.
* **AlgebraicSimplifier (`algebraic_simplifier.cc`)**: Add simplification rules for `kRotate` instructions, including eliminating identity rotations (`norm_shift == 0` or empty shift dimensions) and folding/combining chained `kRotate` operations.
* **HloEvaluator & Constant Folding (`hlo_evaluator.cc`)**: Implement `kRotate` evaluation on literals within `HloEvaluator`, enabling compile-time constant folding (`HloConstantFolding`) of `kRotate` operations on known constant operands.
* **Testing**: Add comprehensive unit tests in `RotateExpanderTest`, `AlgebraicSimplifierTest`, `HloEvaluatorTest`, and `HloConstantFoldingTest`.
